newsitem.title: USA: Cuban exiles laud U.S. move on news groups.
newsitem.headline: Cuban exiles laud U.S. move on news groups.

text.p: The most powerful Cuban exile group on Wednesday welcomed U.S. permission for several U.S. news organisations to open bureaus in Cuba and said it hoped correspondents would report without fear or interference from President Fidel Castro's government.
Ninoska Perez, spokeswoman for the Cuban American National Foundation (CANF), said exiles would be pleased to have independent reports from the communist-ruled island.
"We would like to see it covered from an angle other than the government's," she told Reuters. "So many things are happening in Cuba and sometimes correspondents there now look the other way."
She said she hoped reporters would not be manipulated by the Castro government and avoid critical stories for fear of expulsion.
"We have seen many correspondents put on a plane and sent out," she said.
The Clinton administration announced in Washington on Wednesday that it had granted licenses to 10 organisations to open news-gathering offices in Cuba.
The CNN television network already has permission from Cuba and the relationship of its founder, Ted Turner, with Castro has caused suspicion among anti-communist exiles in Miami.
Perez said CNN executives had met with officials of the CANF, the most powerful of Miami's many exile groups.

"They tried to make it clear they would provide fair coverage and that Ted Turner's friendship with Castro had nothing to do with it. That's what they told us. I hope they do a good job. Time will tell."
But Florida Congressman Lincoln Diaz-Balart mocked CNN and condemned what he said was a renewed crackdown against independent journalists in Cuba.

"How ironic that at the same moment that Castro has organised 'acts of repudiation' by mobs of thugs against Raul Rivero and other independent journalists in Cuba, Castro's friend Ted Turner gets to open a news bureau in Cuba," he said in a statement.

Diaz-Balart, who is close to the exile community, said he hoped the crackdown received as much coverage on CNN as "Castro's preference for the Atlanta Braves got by CNN's principal anchor during the tyrant's most recent trip to New York".

Representative Robert Menendez, whose New Jersey constituency is home to many Cuban Americans, said the decision provided a good opportunity for correspondents to report on human rights and the realities of daily life in Cuba.
"The professional integrity of these news organisations is at stake to responsibly cover both sides of the story in Cuba," Menendez said in a statement.
It was unfortunate Castro had banned satellite dishes which would have allowed the population to watch CNN, he added.
